input_signals.name: Earnings_Yield_When_Capex_Decelerating
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), INDICATOR(SUB(MA(RATIO(capx, at), 3), RATIO(capx, at)), 0))
input_signals.hypothesis: A high earnings yield predicts returns only when management is actively pulling back from its own recent investment pace; cheap firms still spending above their three-year norm are likely value traps with unfinished, low-return projects.
input_signals.reasoning: The indicator switches the valuation signal on exactly when current capex intensity falls below its own three-year average, a firm-specific discipline event rather than a cross-sectional level. This conditional structure tests whether the value premium is state-dependent on investment deceleration instead of merely additive with investment level.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ib, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), indicator( sub( ma( ratio( capx, at ), 3 ), ratio( capx, at ) ), 0 ) )

input_signals.name: Expensive_Externally_Funded_Empire
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(aqc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms trading at high multiples of book that simultaneously fund large acquisitions and equity issuance are exploiting rich valuations to build empires, and subsequently underperform as integration costs and dilution surface.
input_signals.reasoning: The interaction targets the short leg of the story: overvaluation supplies cheap financing, and acquisition plus stock-issuance intensity reveals that management is spending it externally rather than internally. Missing aqc or sstk genuinely means no acquisition or issuance in that year, so treating them as zero is the economically correct convention rather than a coverage patch.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( mul( prcc_f, csho ), ceq ) ), rank( ratio( add( coalesce( aqc, 0 ), coalesce( sstk, 0 ) ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Growth_Premium_Per_Dollar_Invested
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq), TS_SUM(capx, 5)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: The market's premium over book value is an implicit price paid for the firm's expansion program; when investors capitalize each dollar of the firm's cumulative five-year capital spending at a very high premium, expectations for that capital's payoff are extrapolative and subsequent returns are poor, while a small premium per dollar invested marks quietly funded, underappreciated capacity.
input_signals.reasoning: Instead of averaging a valuation rank with an investment rank, this puts the valuation premium in the numerator and the investment program in the denominator, so the signal is a price-per-unit-of-investment quantity that cannot be replicated by either theme alone (a cheap firm with tiny capex and an expensive firm with huge capex can rank identically). Cumulating capex over five years captures the whole program that current expectations are supposedly paying for and smooths lumpy single-year projects; winsorization controls the small-denominator tail.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( mul( prcc_f, csho ), ceq ), ts_sum( capx, 5 ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Own_History_Peak_Valuation_And_Investment
input_signals.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that ramp reinvestment to a five-year high precisely when their own valuation multiple is at a five-year high are timing capital spending to rich equity prices, a behavioral pattern that precedes disappointment; firms investing at their own historical trough while cheaply valued relative to their own history are counter-cyclical allocators that subsequently outperform.
input_signals.reasoning: Both legs are within-firm position-in-own-history measures, so the signal is orthogonal by construction to the cross-sectional level effects that HML and CMA span and instead measures the co-timing of valuation and investment inside the firm. The multiplicative form fires only for the joint peak (or joint trough) state, which is the specific "investing into your own high multiple" mechanism rather than either theme's level anomaly.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ts_rank( ratio( mul( prcc_f, csho ), ceq ), 5 ), ts_rank( ratio( capx, ppent ), 5 ) )

input_signals.name: Cheap_Capacity_With_Rising_Asset_Productivity
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che), ppegt))), RANK(GROWTH(RATIO(sale, ppegt), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm whose enterprise value sits low relative to the gross replacement cost of its installed capacity, and which is simultaneously extracting more revenue per dollar of that existing capacity, is creating value without buying new assets — the disciplined-allocator case — whereas expensive firms with falling revenue per unit of capacity are paying up for idle or unproductive expansion.
input_signals.reasoning: The valuation leg is priced against gross PP&E (a replacement-cost base) rather than book equity or earnings, so it is not the HML ratio, and the investment leg is capital productivity growth rather than capital growth, so it is not the CMA ratio. The interaction is economic: cheapness relative to installed capacity is only informative if that capacity is being used better, which distinguishes disciplined operators from asset-heavy value traps.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( ratio( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), che ), ppegt ) ) ), rank( growth( ratio( sale, ppegt ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Signed_Capex_Discipline_Gated_Earnings_Yield
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), SIGN(SUB(MA(RATIO(capx, at), 3), RATIO(capx, at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A high earnings yield is a genuine bargain only when the firm is spending below its own three-year capex norm; a cheap firm that is spending above its own norm is a value trap pouring capital into a business the market has already marked down, so the two states should sit at opposite ends of one continuous signal.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs the degenerate-portfolio failure of the gen-0 winner: the 0/1 indicator piled every non-decelerating firm onto a single value (no computable long-short stats), whereas the signed gate maps cheap-and-disciplined to the top and cheap-but-accelerating to the bottom, with expensive firms near zero in both states. Because valuation enters non-monotonically (only cheap firms take extreme values), the resulting spread is not a repackaged HML leg and should survive the FF5 benchmark better than a raw value-times-investment product.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ib, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), sign( sub( ma( ratio( capx, at ), 3 ), ratio( capx, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cheapness_Times_Marginal_Return_On_Capex
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ebitda, 1), LAG(capx, 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cheap firms are only underappreciated capital allocators if the capital they did spend actually earned something; incremental EBITDA per dollar of prior-year capex separates disciplined, high-marginal-return investors from cheap firms whose spending generates no incremental profit.
input_signals.reasoning: The investment leg is a *marginal* productivity measure (payoff per dollar of last year's capex), not an investment level or growth rate, so it is orthogonal in construction to CMA and it changes the economic question from "how much do they invest" to "does their investment pay". Lagging capex against contemporaneous EBITDA change imposes the correct causal ordering, and winsorizing controls the small-capex denominator tail that would otherwise dominate the rank.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( delta( ebitda, 1 ), lag( capx, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cheapness_Times_Self_Funded_Surplus
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0))), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A cheap firm is an underappreciated disciplined allocator only if its own operations more than cover its expansion outlays; the surplus of operating cash flow over capital expenditure plus acquisitions, scaled by assets, measures whether investment is internally affordable, and cheap firms with a positive self-funded surplus should outperform cheap firms whose expansion outruns internal cash.
input_signals.reasoning:
The critic was right that omitting operating cash flow left the allocation story ill-posed and that price-scaling the outlay simply reproduced the capital-investment-to-price anomaly, so operating cash flow is now included and the investment leg is deflated by assets rather than by market value — keeping the valuation channel entirely in the separate cheapness leg. The interaction is economic rather than cosmetic: the same investment level is disciplined for a cash-generative firm and reckless for a cash-consuming one, and only the second case is a value trap.

input_signals.name: Cheapness_Times_Investment_Stability
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(VOL(RATIO(capx, at), 5))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Discipline is about the smoothness of capital deployment, not only its level: cheap firms whose capital spending rate is stable across five years are running a planned, return-driven program, while cheap firms with erratic, lurching spending are reacting to conditions and destroy value, so cheapness pays off mainly in the stable-investment group.
input_signals.reasoning: The investment leg is a second moment of the spending rate, which the FF5 investment factor (a level/growth sort) cannot span, so the resulting spread should retain alpha even though the valuation leg is a conventional cash-earnings yield. It also tests a genuinely new notion of "discipline" — predictability of capital allocation — against the level- and change-based notions already in the archive.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ebitda, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( neg( vol( ratio( capx, at ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Expensive_Per_Employee_And_Hiring_Hard
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), emp)), RANK(GROWTH(emp, 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Labor is the largest quasi-irreversible investment for most firms; when the market already capitalizes each employee at a very high value and management simultaneously expands headcount rapidly, the expansion is being justified by a rich valuation rather than by demonstrated unit economics, and subsequent returns are poor.
input_signals.reasoning: This opens an untested investment channel — human-capital rather than physical or acquisitive investment — and pairs it with a valuation metric (market value per employee) that is not a scaled-accounting multiple, so the portfolio's HML and CMA exposures should be far smaller than in the archive's book- and asset-based designs. The interaction is economic: rapid hiring is only a warning sign when the price already embeds a high value per head, and cheap-per-employee firms adding staff are simply scaling proven operations.

input_signals.name: Payout_For_Capex_Substitution_In_Cheap_Firms
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(SUB(DELTA(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), at), 1), DELTA(RATIO(capx, at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The credible signal of a disciplined allocator is an observed reallocation at the margin — raising the share of assets paid out to owners while lowering the share absorbed by capital spending — and this reallocation is most under-priced in firms that already trade at a high earnings yield because the market treats them as stagnating rather than as re-optimizing.
input_signals.reasoning:
The investment leg is a within-firm substitution measure (change in payout intensity minus change in capex intensity), not a level or a growth rate, so it is not a restatement of CMA or of the payout-yield anomaly, and it fires only on the year of the reallocation decision. Missing dvc is genuinely zero payout, so the COALESCE convention is economic, and both differences are asset-scaled to keep the two channels commensurable.

input_signals.name: Growth_Capex_Share_At_Rich_Multiple
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ppent, 1), capx), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital spending decomposes into maintenance and expansion: the fraction of capex that actually shows up as net new plant is the growth share, and richly valued firms whose spending is overwhelmingly expansion rather than replacement are committing irreversible capital to validate their multiple, whereas maintenance-dominated spenders are simply preserving existing cash flows.
input_signals.reasoning:
This replaces the inventory-versus-sales leg, which the critic rightly identified as a published Lev–Thiagarajan fundamental signal, with a decomposition of capex into growth versus maintenance content — a composition measure with no standard anomaly counterpart and one that CMA (an asset-growth level sort) does not distinguish. The interaction is economic rather than mechanical: the same total capex is benign when it replaces depreciating plant and dangerous when a high multiple is being defended with new irreversible capacity.

input_signals.name: Cash_Value_Gated_By_Investment_Burn
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(che, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), SIGN(SUB(ebitda, ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A large cash balance relative to market value is only worth something to shareholders if it is not already committed to expansion; firms whose cash earnings exceed their investment outlays will accumulate or distribute that cash, while cash-rich firms already spending more than they earn are pre-committing the balance sheet to empire building and the apparent cheapness is illusory.
input_signals.reasoning:
Unlike the archived industry z-score wrapper this is a genuine two-way interaction: the valuation channel is balance-sheet liquidity per dollar of price and the gate is a two-sided internal-funding test, so cash-rich burners land at the bottom and cash-rich self-funders at the top while low-cash firms sit near zero. It also avoids the fragile TS_SUM(capx,5) denominator entirely and keeps coverage at the annual-accounting ceiling since ebitda, capx and che are broadly reported and missing acquisitions genuinely mean none occurred.

input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), SIGN(SUB(ebitda, ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What shareholders can actually receive is net cash, not gross cash: firms whose cash exceeds total debt and whose cash earnings more than cover their investment program hold genuinely distributable liquidity, while equally cash-rich but levered firms that outspend their earnings will hand that cash to creditors and to expansion instead.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates one design choice in the archive's only fully sign-consistent signal — replacing gross cash-to-price with net-cash-to-price — which should sharpen the short leg by pushing levered burners to the bottom rather than merely low-cash firms. If the alpha strengthens, the mechanism is distributable liquidity rather than cash balances per se; if it weakens, the effect is about cash hoards being underpriced regardless of leverage, which is itself an informative finding.

The economic upgrade is real rather than cosmetic: transitory surpluses from a capex pause are downweighted relative to a sustained funding policy.

input_signals.name: Cash_Value_Times_Internal_Funding_Coverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(che, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ebitda, ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0))), ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0))), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: The degree to which internal cash generation covers the investment program — not merely whether it does — should scale the mispricing of a cash-rich, cheaply priced firm: a firm earning twice its investment outlay is a materially more disciplined allocator than one that just breaks even, and a firm spending far beyond its cash earnings is the most pre-committed empire builder.
